doc.title: Earl Watkins interviewed by Monk Rowe, San Francisco, California, August 7, 2002

title: Personal experiences of discrimination
summary: Chinatown screens, a bar refusing him in uniform, and a Fillmore miniature golf course that wouldn't sell tickets to blacks.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Segregation on the road and the bandstand

blocks.x: Yeah. I experienced that. That’s not just hearsay. That was my experience. And another experience, during World War II I was playing at the Stage Door Canteen, our St. Mary’s band, Frasier Scott, one of our trombonists and I, we went out for a beer on intermission. And we went to this little, it was patterned after a cable car, a little bar, to get a beer on intermission. And in our uniforms, the uniform of our country, the bartender said, “If you want a drink you’ll have to go out in the Fillmore.” I said, “Well I’d like to see the manager please.” Well the manager was trying to sneak out. And so we got him nailed and we said, “We’re here in the uniform of our country and you won’t serve us?” “Well, well.” He stammered and stuttered, and anyhow we walked out. But there was a lot of —

in this town — I guess maybe after the gold rush, or I don’t know when the color bar maybe got to be broader. But I can remember my experiences, even as a kid, they opened a miniature golf course on Fillmore and Sutter, right into Fillmore, right in the middle of the Western Addition, where most of the people lived. Miniature golf. And they wouldn’t sell tickets to colored.
For moralistic of course it’s terrible but from an economic standpoint it just seems silly. Why would they open it in the Western District as you said?
